new_statements.quote: Another language of the region that also has complex tone specification is Kuke, the language of the Kutang region midway between Tsum and (upper) Nubri. Table 7 shows the contrast present in Kuke; a high fall, a mid fall, a low fall, and a rise-fall complex melody. Table 7: Kuke tone contrasts -- H-fall M-fall L-fall R-fall / Kuke 53 42 31 231. While the Kuke data is suggestive, it is not on its own convincing.
new_statements.citation: Dhakal, Dubi Nanda, Mark Donohue, Bhojraj Gautam & Naijing Liu. 2016. Diagnosing a contact history for Tsum. Nepalese Linguistics 31: 14-20. Kathmandu: Linguistic Society of Nepal. (The running footer on the first page misprints 'Vol. 27, 2012'; the volume front matter reads 'Volume 31, November 2016'. No DOI: NepJOL starts at vol. 33.)
new_statements.locator: p.17 (section 3, right column, with Table 7 'Kuke tone contrasts'); PDF page 21 of the Digital Himalaya volume file; lines 188-201 of the saved extract
new_statements.relation_note: States that Kuke has lexical tone with a 'complex tone specification': four contrastive tones -- a high fall, a mid fall, a low fall and a rise-fall melody, given in Chao numerals as 53, 42, 31 and 231 (Table 7). The Kuke system is adduced as the likely areal ('Manaslu') source of Tsum's atypical eight-way monosyllabic tone system; Table 11/12 class Tsum's tonal phonology as 'not Tibetan.. somewhat atypical' from the Kuke perspective. Nothing is said about word stress or accent in Kuke; no acoustic figures for Kuke; the tone-bearing domain (syllable vs word) is discussed for Tsum only. Companion extract saved: in the same folder.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kuke (Kutang Ghale) is a tone language: four lexically contrastive pitch melodies -- high falling (53), mid falling (42), low falling (31) and rise-fall (231); no statement about word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The article's subject is Tsum (tsum1240, Tibetic), but section 3 presents the authors' own first-hand data on 'Kuke, the language of the Kutang region midway between Tsum and (upper) Nubri' as the proposed contact partner: Table 7 'Kuke tone contrasts' (p.17) and Table 10 'Verbal agreement in Kuke' (p.18), with 'Kuke is not a Tibetan language' (p.18) and 'Kuke, the nearby language of the Manaslu region' (p.19). Kutang-region Kuke of upper Gorkha = Kutang Ghale [ght] = kuta1241 (co-author Gautam is the Kuke fieldworker of Donohue & Gautam 2019; co-author Liu now holds the ELDP Kuke grant). Not Northern/Southern Ghale, not Nubri, not Tsum. Cited in Donohue 2019 (Gipan 4) reference list, which is how it was found; absent from Glottolog's kuta1241 references, from our bibliography and from ROUND1.

sources.citation: Liu, Naijing & Dolma Choekyi Lama. 2026. Kuke Orthography (dated 30 March 2026). 2 pp. In: Documenting Kuke: the linguistic ecology of a 'stolen' language in Nepal, ELAR collection SG1147 (dk0839), bundle ght0123 'Elicitation and orthography', file, hdl:2196/71ghfn3r-8m29-kvrf-zz93-5744amv33haj.
sources.note: No sentence on tone, pitch, stress or accent, and the orthography has no tone marks or tone letters. The only prosody-adjacent text is the (garbled in the original) note quoted below on non-modal/breathy voice and nasalisation. Long vowels are written with 'h' ('h is used for syllable with a single vowel or indicating long vowels, such as in Bihi'). The companion wordlist distinguishes homophonous spellings by indices (da1/da2/da3), which a human should check against the open ght0123/ght0124 recordings for a possible tonal contrast.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2019. A typological investigation of Nepalese languages. Gipan 4: 30-37. Kathmandu: Central Department of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University.
sources.note: No phonology content: a Splitstree neighbour-net over 229 reclassified WALS-style morphosyntactic features for 59 Nepalese languages; Kuke appears with Kusunda and the two Nubri varieties at the typological margin ('closely joined by Kuke, and tenuously connected with Tsum', p.34; non-ergative profile, p.35). The words tone/tonal/stress/pitch/accent do not occur; sec. 6 says 'Further work will involve the comparison of phonological features'.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2014. A note on prosodic contrasts and segmental analysis in Himalayan languages. Unpublished ms., The Australian National University, 11 pp. (PDF metadata title 'Himalayan prosody and phonation revised', created 2014-03-25; file from the author's ANU downloads folder; precursor of Donohue 2018, 'Prosodic contrasts and segmental analysis in Himalayan languages', Australian Journal of Linguistics).
sources.note: Nothing about Kuke / Kutang Ghale: the note does not mention the language (no hits for Kuke, Kutang, Ghale, Bihi, Chhak, Tsum, Nubri, Gorkha, Manaslu). It is a general argument that Himalayan register systems with pitch height + VOT + breathy phonation (Central Tibetan, Dzongkha, Tamang, Padma-bKot Tshangla, Bumthang, Kurtoep, Kyirong, Dongwang) are most economically analysed as two plosive manners (/ph/-/p/) crossed with two (Kyirong: three) contrastive pitch registers, with low register conditioning lower VOT and breathiness; tonal contour contrasts are explicitly set aside (fn. 1).
